'''''Sisymbrium erysimoides''''', known as '''smooth mustard''',<ref>[[Timothy John Entwisle|Entwisle, T.J.]] (1996). Brassicaceae. In: Walsh, N.G.; [[Timothy John Entwisle|Entwisle, T.J.]] (eds), Flora of Victoria Vol. 3, Dicotyledons Winteraceae to Myrtaceae. Inkata Press, Melbourne.</ref>  is a plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]].<ref name=rahman>{{cite journal |doi=10.3390/molecules23010231|title= Brassicaceae mustards: Traditional and agronomic uses in Australia and New Zealand|year=2018 |last1=Rahman |first1=M. |journal=Molecules|volume= 23|issue= 1|page= 231|pmid= 29361740|pmc= 6017612|doi-access= free}}</ref>   It is found on roadsides and wasteland, and as a weed of arable land.  A native to western Mediterranean region, it is now well-established throughout the world.

==Description==
Cool season annual, erect, glabrous or shortly pubescent herb 10–80 cm tall. Basal leaves are up to 15 cm long, [[lyrate]]-[[pinnatifid]], toothed, [[petiole (botany)|petiolate]], reducing to [[lanceolate]], mostly toothed. Flowerheads are [[paniculate]]. [[Sepal]]s are 1–2 mm long and glabrous. [[Petal]]s are 1–2.5 mm long, yellow to pale yellow. [[Siliqua]] are linear, straight, horizontal, 2.5–5 cm long, 1 mm wide and attenuate into a style; [[pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s are thick and 2–5 mm long. Flowering is in late winter and spring.

It was introduced in Australia where it is now widespread in dry regions west of the [[Tablelands Region|Tablelands]].

==Uses==
===In food===
Young leaves are eaten as salad.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://flora.org.il/en/books/plant-stories-2/chapter-e/useful_plants_e2/|title=Edible Leaves and Fruits}}</ref>

===Traditional medicine===
Ethnobotanically used as a medicinal plants for respiratory disorders.<ref name=rahman /><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.jep.2014.08.005 | title=Ethnobotanical uses of medicinal plants for respiratory disorders among the inhabitants of Gallies – Abbottabad, Northern Pakistan | year=2014 | last1=Kayani | first1=Sadaf | last2=Ahmad | first2=Mushtaq | last3=Zafar | first3=Muhammad | last4=Sultana | first4=Shazia | last5=Khan | first5=Muhammad Pukhtoon Zada | last6=Ashraf | first6=Muhammad Aqeel | last7=Hussain | first7=Javid | last8=Yaseen | first8=Ghulam | journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology | volume=156 | pages=47–60 }}</ref> Antioxidant molecules - Apigenin, apigenin-7-O-galactoside, apigenin-7-O-β-rhamnoside, apigenin-7-O-glucuronide, kaempferol, apigenin-7-O-rhamnosyl galactoronide, kaempferol-3-xyloside-7-galactoside, quercetin-6,4′-dimethoxy-3-fructo-rhamnoside, quercetin 4′-methoxy-3-fructo-rhamnoside - were reported to be identified from the plant.<ref name=aljaber>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.jscs.2011.07.004 | volume=15 | title=Review on some antioxidant plants growing in Arab world | year=2011 | journal=Journal of Saudi Chemical Society | pages=293–307 | last1 = Al-Jaber | first1 = Nabilah A. | last2 = Awaad | first2 = Amani S. | last3 = Moses | first3 = John E.| issue=4 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The whole plant extract was reported to have anti-inflammatory and analgesic activities.<ref name=aljaber />
